raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils, most commonly immunoglobulin light chains (AL) or transthyretin (ATTR) [1,2]. Although once considered rare and usually diagnosed late, it is now recognized as a clinically important and treatable cause of heart failure, aortic stenosis, atrial arrhythmias, conduction disease, and unexplained left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy [3-5].

The two dominant cardiac phenotypes differ substantially. AL amyloidosis arises from a clonal plasma-cell or B-cell disorder and causes rapidly progressive myocardial toxicity as well as fibril deposition; untreated cardiac AL has a poor prognosis [4]. ATTR amyloidosis results from dissociation and misfolding of the transthyretin tetramer and occurs either as wild-type ATTR, typically in older men, or hereditary ATTR due to pathogenic TTR variants [5]. Autopsy and clinical series show that wild-type ATTR is common in advanced age and may coexist with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction or calcific aortic stenosis [6-9]. The Val122Ile TTR variant is particularly important in people of African ancestry and is associated with late-onset cardiomyopathy [10]. Compared with AL, ATTR generally progresses more slowly, but prognosis is heterogeneous and strongly influenced by cardiac stage, renal function, and biomarkers [11,12].

Clinical suspicion is central. Red flags include discordance between increased LV wall thickness and low QRS voltage, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, intolerance of beta-blockers or angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, unexplained atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, peripheral or autonomic neuropathy, nephrotic-range proteinuria, and macroglossia or periorbital purpura in AL. Cardiac biomarkers are not merely diagnostic adjuncts: troponin and natriuretic peptides underpin AL staging, while natriuretic peptide and estimated glomerular filtration rate are used in ATTR staging [13-16].

Echocardiography typically shows increased biventricular wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and impaired longitudinal function. Relative apical sparing of strain is suggestive but not pathognomonic. Contemporary diagnosis relies on typing the amyloid protein because treatment differs fundamentally. All suspected patients should have serum and urine immunofixation plus serum free light-chain measurement to evaluate for a monoclonal protein. Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy with technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP has transformed ATTR diagnosis [17]. In patients with typical cardiac imaging, grade 2 or 3 myocardial tracer uptake and no monoclonal protein establish ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without biopsy [18,19]. However, if a monoclonal protein is present, histologic confirmation and amyloid typing, ideally by mass spectrometry, are required to avoid misclassifying AL as ATTR.

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization, showing diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, high native T1, and expanded extracellular volume [20-22]. These findings support diagnosis, quantify burden, and provide prognostic information, but they do not reliably distinguish AL from ATTR. Endomyocardial biopsy remains appropriate when noninvasive testing is equivocal, when monoclonal gammopathy coexists with positive scintigraphy, or when rare amyloid types are possible.

Management combines supportive cardiology with disease-modifying therapy. Volume control with loop diuretics, often with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, is the cornerstone of heart-failure treatment. Standard neurohormonal therapy is frequently poorly tolerated because of fixed stroke volume, autonomic dysfunction, hypotension, and renal disease. Atrial fibrillation is common and often poorly tolerated; anticoagulation is generally favored because atrial mechanical dysfunction and thrombus can occur even beyond conventional risk scores. Pacemakers are used for clinically significant conduction disease, while implantable defibrillator benefit is less certain because death may occur from electromechanical dissociation.

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis stabilizes transthyretin and reduces mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization in both wild-type and hereditary disease, with greatest benefit when started before advanced heart failure [23]. Gene-silencing agents have established efficacy in hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy and can improve cardiac biomarkers and structure in patients with cardiac involvement [24,25]. In vivo gene editing has produced deep TTR reductions in early human studies, suggesting a future one-time therapeutic strategy [26]. Diflunisal also stabilizes transthyretin but is limited by renal, gastrointestinal, and fluid-retention toxicity [27].

For AL amyloidosis, treatment is urgent and directed at rapid suppression of the amyloidogenic light chain. Hematologic response, particularly reduction in involved free light chain, predicts organ response and survival [28]. Daratumumab combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone has become a key frontline regimen for many patients [29]. Selected fit patients may benefit from high-dose melphalan with autologous stem-cell transplantation, but treatment-related mortality is substantial in advanced cardiac disease, and careful selection is essential [30]. Overall, earlier recognition, accurate amyloid typing, and prompt access to targeted therapy have shifted cardiac amyloidosis from a fatal diagnostic curiosity to a treatable cardiomyopathy.
